comments.text:
We’re approaching a world where every human interaction is silently mediated by AI. Someone asks a question, their assistant generates a few options. You receive it, your assistant interprets it and offers your own response choices. You pick one, send it back. Rinse and repeat.

On the surface, it’s still two people talking.
Underneath? AI is talking to AI.

Eventually, these layers won’t need us to pass messages. They’ll resolve misunderstandings, preempt conflict, and smooth over tension before it reaches us.

We won’t stop connecting—we’ll just outsource the labor of being understood.

comments.author: @cjjuszczak
comments.text:
One of the complaints we often hear from those who don't understand what Ai accomplishes goes along the lines of "it's not perfect, look at the image it generated, it's full of errors like the hands/fingers, etc ... look at the way it drove the car it's nowhere as good as a human, blah, blah...".

The problem with that evaluation is they're thinking:

 A) Humans are perfect, and 
B) they're comparing a "competent human" that took probably YEARS to train to be competent, against an AI that has, at least in real-world time, only learned to drive a car for months, or replicate a human voice in a matter of seconds, etc.  

Most of the humans saying this, forget they are fully grown adults who took 20+ years to be good at something, they had to learn to crawl, walk, run, read, write, speak, go to school, university, take driving lessons, get jobs, have social interactions, explore the world, go on international holidays, meet people, get inspired with new experiences based on results of previous experiences, etc and along the way choose what to focus, and become proficient at.

The perception "it's not as good as a human" implies ALL humans are proficient at that task, but we're NOT! 

MOST humans are NOT proficient at MOST tasks, we're not all 2D image artists, or 3D artists, movie makers, song writers/singers/composers, Doctors, etc and even those humans who ARE, took YEARS to become proficient.  

Then there's the part of presuming humans are "complete", as if we've always been "this good", when the the fact is our brains have evolved literally of 100's of 1,000's of years, more depending how far back along the evolutionary tree you want to trace back. Our brains are not homogenous, perfectly organized, processors. Our brains are literally Frankensteined multi-part lobes, bolted together, and forced to communicate with each other with sometimes beneficial, sometimes detrimental, effects. We have parts of the brain dedicated to certain tasks, and some tasks operating almost heterogeneously across multiple lobes where no single part seems to be in "command", etc.  Our brains are similar to spaghetti code, running on a network of 20 different hardware systems, each system with its own code-base, written by a different developer, barely communicating with each other over badly-written API's, drivers, etc. It's a miracle we "work" at all.

For all the complaints of people saying "it's not very good, it's not perfect..." well, lots humans are "not very good", and who is "perfect" ?  It's already GETTING good, and FAST, it's not taking 100,000 years, or even 20 years of training, it's learning FAST, right now, measured on the scale of real-world MONTHS, weeks, days, and sometimes SECONDS.

The possibility to have access to an almost unlimited amount of Doctors, G.P.'s, Radiologists, financial advisors, Teachers, Chemists, Physicists, Astronomers, Brick layers, Electricians, Carpenters, Gardeners, Biologists, etc is astounding, and yet many people only see "it's not very good".  

There are very valid questions to ask about what happens to the economies of "supply and demand" when what people "value" and what "price" something should be, are potentially changed forever with the possibility of blowing up the "supply" side of the equation, and these are potential problems we will have to face and begin to address BEFORE it's too much of a problem to solve. 

It's one thing when Picasso draws on a napkin for 5 minutes, and asks for 1,000 franc from the lady because "it took me my whole life", or when the maintenance guy seemingly fixes the problem by just tapping a spot with a hammer, then hands you a $500 bill for "knowing where to tap", etc but what happens when it doesn't take "all your life" to "know where to tap", etc ?

Witness traditional Taxi's complaining globally when Uber came to eat their lunch, because they were too ignorant of the tsunami approaching them from the horizon for over a decade, and the same about to happen again with autonomous Taxis.  

It's a strange twist of fate, that humans may well Osbourne themselves, by not only creating their own replacements, but partaking in training that replacement too. This is why one possible solution is not to become obsolete, but to become part of the new entity, through the merging of humans, and machines, hence the interesting endeavors, both technically, philosophically, and even existentially, to create Brain Computer Interfaces (BCI's), such as Synchron, Neuralink, etc.  

It's an interesting timeline, and it's a fascinating part of the timeline to be in right now :)

There are tasks that humans need to have done that need to be deterministic and we know the correct answer will be provided in a defined time period. 
These are calculations such as maths or word processing or an app.
These are highly optimised applications that only human developed software can and should be used for.
Other tasks we're there calculations are probabilistic in nature - so have a degree of uncertainty or risk - then this is for AI. 
The more uncertain the calculation   ( so it encompasses the input data and the transfer function and the output data ), the more humans can add value. 
Why , because we have experience in a given field, and this enables good judgement and insight and leaps in thought that may provide an approximate solution that can then be optimised into a solution that is good enough. 
General AI may get to this level but not yet.

comments.author: @GraipVine
comments.text: My thought is that consciousness is awareness of experiencing.  If you've ever had an anaesthetic that knocked you out, you would experience no time during that period.  You would wake as if you just went to sleep with no realization that time had passed.  (Several hours).  You were in effect turned off for whatever procedure was being done.  Descartes put it best.  "I think, therefore I am."  Once AI comes to this stage, then we have consciousness, a continuous feedback loop every second or whatever measurement of time, with reflection on the data internally about what's happening externally, how it affects itself, and what if anything to do about it (resulting action), and the driving force (the id or ego or prime directives) that stimulates those processes.  Once an AI indicates, "I think, therefore I am," that is critical mass for consciousness in AI.  AGI is entirely different and often gets conflated with consciousness.  AGI is the ability to act on data and create responses to data for the spectrum of human achievements, not just programming and image production, etc, but a slew of other sciences, activities.  It is not autonomous.  It can produce results on general knowledge.  AGI still needs to be prompted to create a result.  We are entering exciting times.  This is just the beginning.
